entry.title: Trying to fill my well again
entry.content:
On losing confidence and making things for myself again.

Last week I spectacularly stammered my way through a conversation at work. The frustrating part was, this was something I had researched and worked on for weeks. Something I should have been able to explain in my sleep. But the moment I joined the Slack huddle, the words scattered, tumbling out of my mouth and onto the floor.

I have been feeling a serious loss of confidence over the last few months. I have spent a large part of my time over the last two years building successful things and watching them progress in the world and propagate a belief system I hold. But for all the plaudits the work received, it never truly felt mine.

The work used to go out, and people were excited, even ecstatic, about it; but my well still sat empty.

I am proud of these things! But they did not give me the same feeling I get when doing something just for myself. Like a piece of writing, which I have been doing more of recently. Or a project I poured my heart into a while ago. I keep finding joy in the things I did for myself, long after they have been completed.

A few weeks ago, in a long conversation with a very dear friend and fellow artist, we decided to read The Artist’s Way by Julia Cameron together. Another friend recommended this to me nearly six years ago, and it has been on my radar since, but I just never picked it up.

The current crisis of confidence pushed me into reading it. Over the last week or so, I have been working through the chapters, getting a feel for the book. Like every other book in this genre, it starts with a few detailed, slightly long, and somewhat praise-y pages on why “this” is the best method yet. It also has a few too many references to God for my belief system’s liking.

But as I read through and learn more about the intention behind the book, it has aligned well with me. I consider myself an artist, and everyone around me one too. Maybe repeating it for twelve weeks will finally make me believe it.

The opening chapters ask for something specific. Show up for the next twelve weeks and do the two basic tools the book is built on: three morning pages every day and one artist date every week, trusting that the wanting to create counts on its own.

A good chunk of the early chapters is about the inner critic, the voice that has been running commentary in my head for months now, and the book asks you to catch it and shut it down before it gets a vote. After months of my well feeling empty, a book with an entire idea built around filling the well back up felt aimed directly at me.

This morning I did my first-ever morning pages. Three pages longhand before anything else, no editing, no rereading (I really wanted to). The thing I am most proud of is that I only got distracted twice during those 28 minutes. I am hopeful and skeptical in equal measure, trying to respect the wisdom of the book and keep going. My one worry is how this sits alongside all the other writing in my life.

Honestly, I am out of other ideas too. I want to feel good about the work I create and bring into this world, and this book is the best plan I have right now.

The artist dates are something I am genuinely looking forward to. Something I do for myself anyway, but now it has a name. Hoping it gives my photography more dedicated time, instead of the spare scraps of attention it has been surviving on.

As I wrap up this blog, I feel an urge to keep creating and to pay close attention to the art around me. I am reminded that art is especially necessary now, when those in power are willing to shut down the country’s capital and fundamental institutions are crumbling. Art can help hold those in power to account. So the morning pages continue tomorrow.

entry.title: How petting became my love language
entry.content:
I come from Malegaon, a small town near Nashik. My house was located in a very prominent lane. Whenever I stepped outside the house, every few steps, I would come across a familiar face. I must say that the lane was very lively. But it also carried gossip in the air. For me, the whole lane was full of activities like playing, snacking, and chatting at the katta. I still cannot believe I spent my whole childhood in that lane

When I shifted to Mumbai for further studies, I remember being amazed by the huge crowd around me but being unable to find any familiar faces among them. The streets themselves felt alien, and it was hard for me to find the comfort and belongingness I knew. I would walk with loneliness in my heart

I do have social anxiety, so it’s very hard for me to make friends easily. I masked it well enough to let only a hint of it escape from within me. The newness of the city added to it. I spent many years in Mumbai carrying that feeling inside me until one day, I stopped and started observing the things around me. I started connecting with things that were easy to find, like trees and birds (in this case, mostly crows, as Mumbai is full of them). My eyes were especially drawn to street dogs, as I felt we were carrying similar feelings.

I remember being hesitant to pet a street dog initially. But once I started, I never stopped. Now, no matter which city I am in, I know I won't feel lonely. Seeing them on the street gives me immediate comfort. Sometimes I get affection from them, sometimes I get solidarity from them. I always thank them for their existence and feel sorry for the pain we humans have caused them.

So, this has become my habit, I always look for street dogs. They have taught me something very important, love should flow freely and cannot be limited to a particular family. Love should be easy to find. It doesn't have a particular face. Hence one of my love languages is petting

entry.title: Weekly Notes 41/2026
entry.content:
This week was good. I got back to my routine after two weeks of travel and a hectic schedule. Work is progressing well; I did two P.T. sessions, a game, and a run walk. I am still away from a five day active week. But I think I am consistently reaching three to four day active weeks, which isn’t bad. We are in the last quarter of the year (actual year?), I have lots of things to close before the year ends. I think it’s going to be a hectic but fruitful year end.

  • I have been building many of my projects in public for a long time, but not all my work can be public, and not every team I work with works that way. Still, I’ve found a pattern that works for most teams and for me: something like open office hours, except we’re all working. I call it Katte – The Open Desk. We meet online at a specific time, in one or two hour blocks, ideally with 2 to 8 people, and work together or separately, talking only when it helps. It’s mainly meant for teams, but it can also work with strangers as a form of accountability. This week I documented it.
  • A friend, Bharathi, at NPTEL/CODE turned 50. It seems like she is just getting started, even after achieving so much. She is such an inspiration to me.
  • I attended a lecture by Peggy Mohan at APU today. It was brilliant and also fun. She is such a brilliant storyteller.
  • We are making great progress at Dristi V2. The last two weeks were spent designing. It’s been build and build week. The next few weeks will be the same, I guess. Once it reaches some stage, I will share more details.
  • Uthara and Dave from BuzzWomen wrote a book, The Buzz Way, covering how they work. Congratulations, Uthara and Dave.
  • Tomorrow, October 10th, is a big deal; I am guessing based on how far the Delhi police will go to prevent the peaceful protests. If they were this proactive in general, Delhi wouldn’t have become the crime capital. I am very optimistic about the protests; they are going to be large, effective, and, above all, peaceful.
  • NCF is 30 years old now. They are celebrating with lots of programming; attend if you can. Aleph Alpha has built Savanna, a model factory that implements the entire training pipeline in code so that models can be built collaboratively. They have also released their open-weights model, Kolibri. I haven’t tried it yet, but it looks interesting. I came across RoadStr, decentralized road-event reporting using Nostr and MeshCore. Web and Android. It’s very close to the project I had proposed at FOSSHack/2026. I am trying it in a browser now. I will definitely try it on OSMAnd using their plugin. I need to see if I can collect historical data for a specific location for research. Otherwise, it looks great. I am also studying and exploring the Reticulum Network. It seems useful and stable, especially when the bandwidth needs are small.

entry.title: aerodynamic hearses (gang gang)
entry.content:
"[I]n the recent past we have had the aerodynamic style, which has been applied not only to aeroplanes and cars but to electric irons, perambulators and armchairs. On one occasion I even saw an aerodynamic hearse, which is about as far as the aerodynamic style can go (speeding the departing guest?)."

Bruno Munari

I looked up some aerodynamic hearses after this, to see if people still make them.

Someone also figured that they might as well throw out the dead person in the back and go faster.

Some hearses just need to be grand and not fast. Here's one I saw recently.

There's a school of thought common among designers or artists that say that the above hearses are a monstrosity. They lack coherence, in the sense that its form does not follow its function—or as Munari would say, it is as though a fig is growing out of willow trees. There's something distressing about it.

I think I'd agree that beauty comes from when form follows function. But I do think that there is some function involved with a gawdy gold-and-black hearse that looks like both a gang vehicle and an amusement park ride at the same time. Whoever did this was trying to convey something. It is trying to convey their vision of what the journey of death should look and feel like. Maybe the execution is not quite right. It is hard to express. We can be more curious about it as a society.

entry.title: how to sleep
entry.content:
Some people can seemingly sleep at will, and it comes as naturally to them as eating or walking. I am not of this tribe. In the years before there was a general "sleep awareness" in society, I used to have pretty bad sleep, something that occurred to me only in hindsight. I remember being quite sleepy and inattentive in school and college. I thought this was a natural consequence of these institutions being dreadfully boring. Which is true, but I also wasn't good at sleeping. Most of my problem was being able to fall asleep. No one teaches you how to sleep.

I have, over the years, developed a sleep technique that works reasonably well for me. It obviously depends on how well I have done "sleep prep"—the usual popular advice about timing when to eat, avoiding caffeine, wind-down rituals etc. But on a good day, my process of falling asleep takes around 15 minutes.

This is roughly how it works:

  • Sleep is not like a dog on a leash that you tug to get it to walk with you. Sleep is like a cat. I must sit still, I must not think of the cat or gesture at it. Play a little hard to get, and only then may the cat may come to your lap.

  • Focus on the breath, and gravity. Let stray thoughts pass like clouds, but do not become the thought. When you do this right, the thoughts eventually run out, you let muscles relax, until you feel as weighty as a wet towel on a kitchen counter.

  • There may be temptations to shift positions because the current one doesn't feel "quite right." In most cases I remind myself that I won't die if I don't shift positions. Sometimes that thought makes the discomfort go away, much in the same way one may realise they are not drowning because the pool is 4 feet deep. If the discomfort is real and continues despite it, I permit shifting positions—it's not worth resisting these things and having fights in your own head about this.

  • Getting to the wet-towel phase is the most important part. Once you are there, there isn't anything to do. To keep the nothingness going, I look at patterns of shifting shadows in my closed eyelids, along with sounds. It has the same kind of feeling as staring into a flame. At this point, sleep sets in.

entry.title: I am sorry I don’t have a D
entry.content:
It’s 10am and I am making my way to the metro station entrance, I go through the security check-in entrance. And decide to go through the women’s line because I know how things work, you step in a covered makeshift closet, they pass the scanner around you and let you go.

Going through the gent’s line seems scarier, the mistakes feel public, the people are waiting visibly, the wait is visible. God forbid, something triggers off the beep on that detector.

Back to the moment, three guards talk to me loudly with alert commanding voices that I am in the wrong queue, I don’t have a template reaction for this, I am confused, I mumble a “no” and they are all looking at my chest to understand. After two long minutes of confusion, I scan my bag and go my way. The security-guard apologies. I mumble an “it’s okay” and rush to catch the leaving metro.

Although it has happened often enough now for me to expect, but I often am taken by surprise. Broken from my thought, the very thing I was mediating on, a thought lost to time and moment, something I won’t be catch again. Sad. Tragic. The cost is real. Read more about it on Page 9 of A Room of One’s Own by Virginia Woolf.

Can I please pass through the metro line without having to explain myself or my existence?

Being gender-non-conforming has its price in the everyday encounters of life, passing through the metro line, being stopped at washrooms, being gently and mockingly informed of “This is the ladies restroom”.

I also think it’s familiarity, if I had grown up using the men’s restroom with my dad, I might have easily gone to the other one, but I don’t know the unsaid protocols and rules, you pick up silently.

Playing the gender game seems to be the only option, I am…not trying pass as anything, I am just trying to exist as myself.
i can’t change an entire system where they would be respectful while checking boys. I’d take the boys line if it’s easy.

i was confused, because, rationally to me, why or for what benefit would I specially go out of my way to enter a women’s line or a bathroom?
like I don’t know what’s the worse that could happen if they let a boy or two pass through the women’s security check-in?

It is messed up, I don’t have solutions.

And this problem seems to be staying here for the long-term.

The few times I have gotten a pass was because my mom was with me or some female shaped person was vouching for my feminity, that feels wrong on so many levels that I need a gaurantor to pass through the world.

i think am just upset realising the long term effects, am just as upset as I realised that I will be menstruating for the rest of my goddamn life and calculating all the swimming classes or games periods I will miss. And the number of days that will be gone in this.

In the last week, I got called out, mocked or pestered for all of this:

– Metro security check-in
– Going to my berth in the Sleeper bus, the conductor was pissed off because he thought I was using somebody else’s name/gender to get the seat.
– The bus stopped at some random hotel for a restroom break, it’s raining, all the guys are peeing in the corner in the rainwater, I figure out the ladies restroom, I get told off “this is ladies”, this is where I snap, “I am LADIES”, I lie, if I had a dick, I would be happily peeing in the rain, goddamit.
– Using the paid women’s restroom, the money-collector women said something haughtily in a different language and started laughing. I didn’t have time for that, I had to use the restroom.
– I catch a public bus to go the village, I go up to climb the women’s section, it’s full, the college girls are trying to figure out if I am a girl or a guy, they tell me if I am a college student, the fare is free, I nod and smile at them. The bus halts at a stop, the conductor rushed to ticket me, looks confused, asks “If I am ladies”, I say “yes”. Going to the back in men’s department, lugging my suitcase, figuring out the cash exchange would be problematic. I lie again.

entry.title: Chronic pains and plastic brains
entry.content:
I have had a flexible body all my life. I was flexible as a child, like one of those weird ones that could do party tricks, and my friends would always be worried about my skinny arms snapping in half at any moment (they did not so far, Rujula, it's all good). I didn't have any big injuries, but I avoided playing rough at school. I had a rather pain free childhood. Fast-forwarding to right after COVID, my first work trip after a year of mostly sitting brought a herniated disc and debilitating back pain, and after it (somewhat) healed it turned into a recurring pain which came and went truly as it pleased. Lifted something heavy? Back pain. PMS? Back pain. A great day of focused work? Back pain. Maybe my back is weak, let's try to strengthen it with some exerci– back pain. I went to doctors who prescribed MRIs and X-rays and blood tests and ECGs but the back pain was smart enough to go away sometimes to trick me into reporting to the doctors that the pain was better and that their job was done, but it would come back always. I learned to avoid things that may trigger the Big Back Pain, and my brain began to anticipate a small pang of pain as a given whenever I'd bend down or sneeze.

Most recently I pulled a muscle in my hip and it was the most pain and weakest I had felt in a while. I decided to go to a different doctor, one who specialized in chronic pain, and he meant serious business. He identified that I was hypermobile, he prescribed physiotherapy and interferential therapy for the pain, and aquatic therapy and kinesthetic taping for the hypermobility and its complications. After a month of following everything to a T, it's the first time in years I've felt like I'm not constantly in pain.

Pain is a weird thing, it's made up by your brain. The wonderful Hannah Fry and Michael Stevens talked in their podcast about how pain is less an objective sensation and more a conclusion created by the brain to signify danger. The science behind it is very interesting: although it is of course more complicated than this, pain is felt in the body due to signals from a particular type of nerve called nociceptors which are specifically pain receptors, so a signal from these receptors make the brain sense pain regardless of if there is actually anything dangerous happening. But since these receptors often fire when there is something that could be dangerous, the brain looks for the source of danger and deals with it. It's as much an emotional experience as it is a physical one. It's why a band aid on a non-existent wound can alleviate pain for a child who has just stubbed their toe, or why we sometimes don't feel as much pain if we are distracted by the TV. So imagine my surprise when in my first session of physiotherapy my therapist massaged a knot out of my lower back and I instantly felt 80% of my pain disappear. I was suspicious. No way my pain went away in an hour. In my second session she told me that I don't have sciatica pain like I had told her previously, because if I did I would be exhibiting other symptoms. By my third session she had convinced me that most movements were safe to do and my body was just protecting me from the possibility of injury, especially because my first time injuring myself after the work trip was so bad. She reassured me that we had worked on waking up the right muscles so that I won't injure myself and that I should try to gently push myself, and by the end of that session had restored my range of motion to almost double of what I used to be able to do; I can almost touch my feet standing up now! No herniated disc related pain at all. The pain was structural at some point, but over the years it turned neuroplastic. My brain was perpetually sounding the pain alarm and I learned to avoid anything that might cause pain instead of avoiding anything that might cause damage. My brain was just holding my poor body hostage in panic the whole while since the herniated disc. My brain never needed pain killers and MRIs, it needed a hug.

Every day since then I have been rediscovering that telling my body that it is safe, it is cared for, and it can relax yields a deeper stretch and more movement. I have been experimenting with the awareness of pain too, as during my most recent period instead of resisting the cramp I just let it in and felt it in my belly (shoutout to Calra's post on unclenching) and the pain... was still there but honestly it was bearable. It felt like a slow, deep burning inside my belly and I watched it pass beneath me, and my body and brain reassured each other that it's not the worst thing in the world. I'm able to understand the mechanics of my back simply because I'm paying more attention and not freaking out at the slightest pain, and the understanding has lead to more exercises that actually work. Don't get me wrong, the whole process has been truly exhausting because it feels like I'm spending 80% of my time and energy being aware of and thinking about the sensations felt in my body, but I have faith that it's gonna become second nature. I will report back in a month or a year or a decade, but until then I am just grateful my sneezes don't hurt anymore.

entry.title: I love writing but I don't love having to think too much about what I write about - A shotgun approach to writing and editing blogs
entry.content:
Writing is amazing

I fell in love with the hobby of blogging primarily because of the IWCB folks. The fact that I know atleast a few people check out my what I write is rewarding in itself. As such I want to write more not because of validation but because I have all these thoughts rattling around inside my noggin and it's fun to put them down somewhere, and I want to inflict my thought process onto whomever is reading.

Shotgun System

My writing system is called the shotgun system by me. It is simply put banged out in a short burst and shipped for your eyeballs with mostly minimal edits because I write with my editorial eyes.

The reason I do this is because I am passionate about what I write about, but if I am staring at a blank page for more than 5 mins I will not magically write down my thoughts. In fact what is more likely is that whatever I am writing about and whatever my thoughts are about the topic have poofed away into the ether. I have a bad memory, sue me.

I might be opinionated but like most people writing down an essay explaining my opinions is something which induces an anxiety which cause what I will collioquially call "thought constipation" I know it's a crude term mostly made to make you laugh, again sue me for writing for an audience.

I had to delete 4 drafts yesterday for some old prompts which I partially wrote because I could not recapture what my brain felt while reading said prompt. The shotgun approach also has an advantage here, I am not married to ideas which might sound interesting because if I decided to sit down and write a magnum opus with my skills as they currently stand the only thing you will be receiving is jack and shit.

So the shotgun is used again, ideas I am not passionate about are taken to the back of the shed, shown a beautiful sunset and then the delete button is hit.

It's an aggressive way to write, kill your darlings and all.

Anecdotally though, I know that in the time I spend writing the blognum opus I could just write down 7-8 blogs which I have more fun writing and you might have some fun reading.

For me writing is a lot like stimming, i just write down my stream of consciousness. So in a lot of ways you are mainlining my brain.

Should you adopt this system

Yeah for sure. I think writing down blogs is fun, and for non technical opinion posts or even shitposts this approach is fun. The thing is that putting words onto the screen is the goal, and having fun is the reward. If this system lets you maximize having the fun of blogging about your life and the things which are happening around you, then by all means please take the shotgun and say "Hell yeah!"

Write more and have fun.

entry.title: My ongoing battle with burning throat
entry.content:
I've a health story to share, so health insurance agents (human or not), this is the end of the post, thanks for reading!

     

     

Yeah now that we are in the false sense of security, let's talk about it. Every year since catching covid-19, my understanding of my throat pain has been evolving.

First, I thought it was long covid. To be honest covid was very scary to me, and I was trying every precaution I could think of: preventing community spread, masking, sanitizing, even reheating food. If you can read this post you know what all we all went through during that time. So when I finally caught it, long covid as an answer to my throat pain made sense to me, it was temporally correlated, and even my doctors agreed that it seems like my body is "over-reacting" with an inflamed throat. I was prescribed Proton Pump Inhibitors as a treatment for GERD (Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease), a condition that commonly causes acid reflux and heartburn, however it was futile, and no amount of "wait for 6 weeks and then come back" seemed to work.

Elimination diet was the next cure, to the point where I was basically consuming lentils and rice with salt, and hot ginger water daily (yup, that's it). This seemed to work on some days but not on others. Raising the headrest of my bed (stacking a pillow underneath the mattress), staying upright for long. Unfortunately this was not it, and my mood was getting quite worse over time, understandably so.

I got endoscopy done, which is essentially deep throating a camera rod, so yeah, two thumbs down, and it turned out to be fine but with signs of H. pylori. This is a nasty bacterium that supposedly half of the world already has. Why was I having it so bad then? Antibiotics ensued. These were equally nasty with horrible metallic taste for a week with a big dollop of bloat-galore tummy. While my symptoms weren't fully cured, I was told it can take some time as your gut has to readjust. I thought this was it, I just need to "wait for 6 weeks and come back". While I felt better (could be placebo), my symptoms were still erratic and came back from time to time.

So, now I was really nervous and was trying desperate things. I heard of mastic gum, raw garlic (ugh), and "don't take stress" as legitimate advice, although paired with diaphragmatic breathing. Curiously, I also had to travel a bit during this time and eat non-GERD-friendly foods, but I actually felt better, as if I never had any issue. It really felt like I cracked it finally, mastic gum + raw garlic + change of scenery was all I needed.

Or so I thought, months later, a good cup of strong coffee would again trigger my inflamed throat back. I just accepted that it is one of those things that happen to you in your 30s. Your body just fails unexpectedly and you just deal with it. I started consuming more flowery teas, and it was largely working out well.

But then lately, I figured out something once again. Somehow coffee at home is much worse for me but not the ones I would have in cafes, no matter how strong they were. I thought maybe it's the kind of coffee I am consuming, and I tried playing with certain types, but no, it would matter very less. Even tea would cause that at times.

And then, one day, it hit me as my lips got burnt while sipping my own coffee. Since covid, I had switched to microwaving water/coffee to save on time, one less utensil to wash, and the general idea that it would kill all the germs. I found the perfect time it would take to get the water boiling, the perfect temperature to avoid soy milk from boiling over, so that I have the hottest drink possible at home.

As I was literally licking my wounds, it hit me, if a sip can damage my mouth so much, what might be happening to my throat? I also have a terrible learned behaviour from my childhood of consuming food fast (almost like I am a great child for always finishing first, never causing stress to my parents with slow eating), so not only I was drinking very hot coffee, I was also consuming it fast. This thought made me quite upset, that somehow I've been able to just assume burnt lips are just part of life, and hotter the coffee the better it is, and the lukewarm frothy coffee of cafes are to be looked down upon. Many Indians love their hot beverages boiling hot, no matter how hot the day is.

However, a microwave is not the same as a pot on a stove (or induction in my case). A microwave can superheat water beyond 100C when it is heated on its own in a clean cup, something you might have experienced if you microwaved a cup of water only to see it calm as if nothing happened, but the moment you dropped a tea bag it would explode. This made me wonder whether I was consuming drinks much hotter than I realised. Also the act of pouring it from the pot to room temperature cup further cools your average beverage, but I had at times opened the microwave door and taken a sip right away (being so sure I've cracked the perfect timing). As a fool who is very good at suppressing feelings and pain, I believed it to be completely normal.

Maybe it's a little bit of everything, but I have surely learnt that I have the capability to mask my pain, and I should pay attention to my body, even if the signal is weak. As I write this, I again feel so sad and angry at my own self. Who knows what all I have normalised and might be tormenting my body with?

For now, I appreciate lukewarm drinks, bland foods (shoutout to England). May your esophaguses be cool. May you pause and observe your body better.

NOTE: Please don't take health advice from a random blog on the internet. There may be a scientific explanation, but humans can withhold information, even from themselves.

entry.title: My impossible bucket list
entry.content:
New blog post, and as you can guess, Indie Web represent.

So the prompt for this session I chose is "My impossible bucket list". Before I talk about what I mean by "my" or "impossible" or "bucket" or "list", which are all indeed very thought provoking words now that I think of it, let me just jump straight into it (don't worry ramblings will soon ensue).

🔗visa-free travel/stay anywhere

I really really wish boundaries were just paperwork for governments, but not for people who live on the land. If I were a bird, I would go around the planet many times over, find my favourite tree, favourite breeze, favourite smell, favourite sunset, favourite every single thing all across the globe. If I were a (lone) wolf, I would ideally like to move around, go on my own chosen pilgrimages, learn the different terrains, climates, flora and fauna, and enjoy the privilege of being on this planet, no matter how it is. It is funny that the boundaries limit humans from moving, and "immigration" has been a problematic thing since the time of Moses (and perhaps before). I hope the 21st century gives up with the national identities and simply lets people find their own tribe. So much of our life is decided by our place of birth and parenting, it would be great if we could make it easy to try different things without quarter life crisis and intense therapy bills.

🔗an end to factory farming of animals

STOP! I mean, just look at the numbers. Billions of humans end up causing more than 80 billion land animals and tens of billions of farmed fish to be killed every year. The number of wild fish killed is much harder to estimate. Yes we live in the modern world where "food chain" is a risible concept, for we can mass produce sentient beings only to extract their milk, honey, fur and flesh, but may I offer an alternative way of modernity that is far more efficient (plant farming vs plant farming for animal farming) and empathetic (raising animals for food requires higher net consumption of plants). Factory animal farming is just an extremely appalling scale of mass slaughtering.

🔗universal basic income, or "free lunch" for all.

In the year of our (evil) lord 2026, I don't see why not. Religious sites and various shelters/kitchens are able to do it without any complicated math, I don't see why this can't be mandated. Free public transport has also been experimented. Let's just make surviving late stage capitalism a tad bit easier without survival crisis post layoff.

🔗high speed rail everywhere

Let's just make commercial (and private) planes a specialty mode of transport. They are painful to endure, no matter if it's a 40 minute flight or 17 hour flight, the entire airport is just an anxiety producing machine. East Asia has it figured out, a person living in Taipei can commute for work to Kaohsiung (350 km) thanks to High Speed Rail (in 1.5 hours). Imagine Bengaluru to Hyderabad (575 km) in 2.5 hours of a calm, relaxing train journey?

🔗indoctrination to authentic living from childhood, not bad-faith

Why can't we not raise humans to live in good faith by default? Let's give it a go maybe? My first 3 decades have been installing and uninstalling the software of "do as told". I never learnt that I should do because I feel so. Can't we teach authenticity and compassion at the same time? Do we really think authentically raised children will always become entitled narcissistic assholes, who would end up abusing the laws, committing multiple felonies, war crimes, and the rest of the population would just sit back and let them rule the world because they were taught to act in good faith and self actualize? Huh.

🔗to wake up on a moon of Jupiter or Saturn

I really get scared of vast oceans (TIL it's called Thalassophobia, and I've already forgotten it). Like waves the size of a 4 storey building, chills! Now imagine waking up and seeing a huge planet cover your entire perspective as you draw your curtains. Not just an ordinary planet, but one with enormous storms, much bigger than the size of your entire planet, flowing very slowly, with equally large thunders. Why do I want this? Maybe sometimes I want things I am terrified of. Why do I think it's impossible? Radiation alone will kill me.

🔗promised ramblings;

my: How do I know what is "mine". Just because "my" brain thought so, doesn't mean it is "my" thought. What if I am performing? What if I am doublethinking? What if I am acting in bad faith and saying I want things but secretly I think these are the good things, nay, right things to want?

impossible: I mean, we have Virtual Reality and deep-fried DLSS 5 now. Maybe anything is possible in some form. As it is, we all live in false reality anyway, constructed by corporations. I am sorry to burst your bubble but the internet is far from reality, yet we spend most of our time surfing the web.

bucket: Okay fine, I don't have much to say about buckets. I prefer showers. This probably speaks of the privilege of having running water taps 24x7 and not having to live in constant anxiety of water tanker emptying out. I take quick showers, in fact, my childhood has made me quick with everything, but yes, here be privileges.

list: This one is tricky to ramble on, but let me try. What is a list really? I can change every single item of the list, would it still be the same list? What if my bucket list changes over time? Does that mean a list is always becoming, never finite? Is our list an atelic project?

entry.title: How The Preamble I Edited Reached Our Clinic in Physical Form
entry.content:
When you come to Arali Health Centre, you will be greeted by this beautiful framed preamble.

If you look closely, you can see something interesting about it.

For reference, here is how the original preamble looks in the 1950 Constitution, from the copy preserved by ServantsOfKnowledge on archive.org:

The words “socialist”, “secular”, and “and integrity” were added only in the 42nd amendment of the Constitution in 1976. And therefore, the original preamble doesn’t have it.

The original preamble came with beautiful artwork as you can see. According to Lalit Kala Akademi, the art work on this page is by Beohar Rammanohar Singa. They also say how the calligraphic writing in the Constitution is by Prem Behari Narayan Raizada, but I’m not sure who among them wrote the text on the preamble page. In any case, it is handwritten.

So, after 1976, people had two choices when they had to show the preamble anywhere. Either use the original preamble with the artwork (which would be outdated because of the amendment), or show the updated preamble without the artwork.

If you’ve seen NCERT textbooks, you’ve probably seen one version like this:

You may also have seen some variants that try to preserve as much art

It is in this context that on 21 April, 2024, I wanted to run a campaign to put preamble as profile picture for Indian general election.

I wanted to preserve as much art from the original preamble as possible and decided to do my own editing in GIMP.

I noticed that all the letters I needed for SOCIALIST and SECULAR where already present in SOVEREIGN DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC JUSTICE EQUALITY. Similarly, “and integrity” could be built from nearby words.

By hand-picking letters and constructing words, one could do justice to the handwritten original.

The watermark had to be restored which I did by picking up a vector of the emblem of India and placing it in places where the original didn’t have it (because of text overlay).

Eventually, I ended up with this:

My friend Subin had made a fun video of me explaining this process.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by lnstaɡram User (@subins2000)

When I started the profile picture campaign, Vinay Kumar of Reclaim Constitution immediately noticed what I had done.

After a few months, I received this message from Vinay:

Here is the link to the Wikimedia Commons file.

Since Wikipedia comes up when people search for preamble, and the page has been edited to include this edited preamble version, people are now using this for making preamble themed gifts.

And yesterday, Swathi spoke at the book discussion organized by APCR.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by APCR Karnataka (@apcrkarnataka)

After the talk she received the framed preamble as a memento.

And that is now adorning the wall of our clinic.

entry.title: Surveys
entry.content:
I don't trust any quoted statistics by default because I've (anecdotally) realised that pretty much every study is sloppily done or misinterpreted when quoted. The only time I trust a statistical analysis is when I have personally looked into it and seen that they did things right. I'm not even a stats pro or anything, the bar is in hell and any AI model, when given sufficient data and reasonably good prompting can debunk things pretty well.

The other day, I spoke to a data scientist who worked on surveys. He spoke about how a reputed survey firm they hired that's been around for over half a century that can't do the most basic things right. The kind of problems are unfathomably bad—the class of errors is stuff like asking the questions in a language that's not of a specific town, finishing the questions in impossibly fast times, not actually going to any household, etc.

In this case, this person had to throw close to half of the data points away because they were suspect. This just happened to be a person who cared enough to look into the data, no one in their organisation was particularly asking to do these checks. If it were a person who cared a little less and didn't add friction to their own work because of it, we would have a survey were millions of people would have been essentially lied to.

Most analyses are based on bad data, based on bad assumptions, processed in bad ways to give a totally bad result in ways that cannot even cancel each other out.

Actually let me pull out the classic:

However, I am pretty excited about AI being able to help me interpret and understand data and studies better. If used correctly, it's great for being able to do the unreasonable effort to wade through sloppy analyses, and I find myself doing that a lot more often. In the past, I would just kind of assume a default "probably false" and move on, which often leads to missed opportunities to actually learn things about the world.

entry.title: The Goal
entry.content:
“You say your plant uses robots?” he asks.

“In a couple of departments, yes,” I say.

“Have they really increased productivity at your plant?”

“Sure they have,” I say. “We had—what?” I scan the ceiling for the figure. “I think it was a thirty-six percent improvement in one area.”

“Really … thirty-six percent?” asks Jonah. “So your company is making thirty-six percent more money from your plant just from installing some robots? Incredible.”

I can’t hold back a smile.

“Well…no,” I say. “We all wish it were that easy! But it’s a lot more complicated than that. See, it was just in one department that we had a thirty-six percent improvement.”

Jonah looks at his cigar, then extinguishes it in the ashtray.

“Then you didn’t really increase productivity,” he says.

I feel my smile freeze.

“I’m not sure I understand,” I say.

Jonah leans forward conspiratorially and says, “Let me ask you something—just between us: Was your plant able to ship even one more product per day as a result of what happened in the department where you installed the robots?”

I mumble, “Well, I’d have to check the numbers …”

“Did you fire anybody?” he asks.

I lean back, looking at him. What the hell does he mean by that?

“You mean did we lay anybody off? Because we installed the robots?” I say.

“No, we have an understanding with our union that nobody will be laid off because of productivity improvement. We shifted the people to other jobs. Of course, when there’s a business downturn, we lay people off.”

“But the robots themselves didn’t reduce your plant’s people expense,” he says.

“No,” I admit.

“Then, tell me, did your inventories go down?” asks Jonah.

I chuckle.

“Hey, Jonah, what is this?” I say to him.

“Just tell me,” he says. “Did inventories go down?”

“Offhand, I have to say I don’t think so. But I’d really have to check the numbers.”

“Check your numbers if you’d like,” says Jonah. “But if your inventories haven’t gone down … and your employee expense was not reduced … and if your company isn’t selling more products—which obviously it can’t, if you’re not shipping more of them—then you can’t tell me these robots increased your plant’s productivity.”

In the pit of my stomach, I’m getting this feeling like you’d probably have if you were in an elevator and the cable snapped.

The Goal by Eliyahu Moshe Goldratt is hokey. It's hammy, cheesy, and schlocky. It is vintage, artisanal eighties cornball slop. It's drowning in awful dime-store, rinky-dink writing. It is prescient. It is full of powerful ideas. It has transformed industries. It is effective. It destroyed Goldratt's career, and then transformed it. It has a dedicated fanbase. It has made him a guru to the industry. But I suspect it has, despite everything, not actually had its ideas applied as much as it should have.

If you judge a book by the cover, the cover of my used copy I found in a used book store1 nails the feel.

There's the ugly highlights, the gaudy plating of the type, the messy composition, the culty portrait—and yet—I can't look away. There's a certain artfulness to the christmas tree-esque chart taking us towards the north star, The Goal.

So, what exactly is The Goal?

It is a business thriller novel about a plant manager, Alex 'Al' Rogo of UniCo who needs to save his factory in his hometown of Bearington. But it is a vehicle for what later became Goldratt's Theory of Constraints. This is what the synopsis in my faux-jacket inner fold says.

Written in a fast-paced thriller style, The Goal is a gripping novel, which is transforming management thinking throughout the world. [...]

It is a book to recommend to your friends in the industry – even to your bosses – but not to your competitors.

Okay, so what is actually "the goal" that the title, The Goal is referring to?

The goal that The Goal refers to is making money. No, really. The book literally spells this out, several times. The goal is to make money now, and in the future. I appreciate the clarity. There is a whole chapter where Al sits down by the hillside overlooking his soon-to-be-doomed factory as he contemplated the smooth aluminium finish of his Bud, wondering what "the goal" is. The whole chapter is him listing out all possible candidates for what "the goal" is, until he has an a-ha moment where he realises the goal is to make money. This is the conclusion that sets forth the events that save his factory, all sprawled out across its 350-odd pages.

Before I forget to mention this—yes there's also terrible romance subplot around the protagonist's failing marriage.

This book is a richly cartoonish, warm, and sickly synthetic world. I visualised every scene coloured like an eighties hollywood B-movie. It really adds to the atmosphere where people talk in large meeting round tables where people are smoking cigars, or when the protagonist is fighting with his wife who just got her hair frizzed up. There's the Dilbert-esque boss who has a loose temper, the hardworking inventory woman with glasses, the impatient pot-bellied production manager, the old grumpy chief accountant, and of course our smart and relatable protagonist.

It is in this world where Al Rogo serendipitously gets in touch with his former physics teacher, an Israeli man named Jonah, who is mysteriously seen talking to people in expensive suits and getting into limos. Jonah is the principled socratic mentor, sharp and frustrating, but through his methods, catalyses the protagonists to think for themselves and save the factory.

It feels like it has no right to work, but it does. Goldratt, through his various characters walk us through powerful systems thinking ideas. There is plenty of literature out there on the Theory of Constraints, and systems thinking as applied to business and management processes out there. But I was amazed to see ideas about the dynamics of systems under various constraints and bottlenecks in here explained this straightforwardly.

Donella Meadows' Thinking in Systems has been quite an influence for me, it is a book that has similar kinds of ideas, explained elegantly. It is what solidified my core belief that the world is malleable, and full of opportunities. But this book clearly appeals to someone who thinks like me, who likes things formulated in a specific, nerdy and analytical kind of way. It is effective for me. When explained to others, it is often received with some fascination and nodding, but in my career, I have rarely seen it applied directly and effectively. Time and time again, in the software engineering projects I've worked in, people regularly fall into all kinds of systems traps of the kind you'd see in the UniCo factory. Nothing has changed since the eighties.

I myself had once given a talk on this topic earlier this year at an AI conference after noticing how ineffectively we are utilising AI agents in our workplaces. I never felt that I was quite effective in getting my message across. It wasn't easy enough. Goldratt is able to exploit the aesthetics of warm, cozy slop, callbacks to familiar cliches, to deliver his theories with clarity and a certain obviousness (so much so, that The Goal has been criticised for being "too obvious"). It is effective, in all sorts of ways that my talk could never be. And all of this is expressed quite earnestly.

It was a pretty non-consensus idea, and noted for its clunkiness even at the time of publication. My book has an afterword from Eliyahu himself, reflecting on this book, twenty years after publication. It is a striking essay. The book started out as a way for him to explain the concepts behind a software he was selling. His journey was rough, and in this essay he throws massive shade at his own employees and even his co-author Jeff Cox.

Out of desperation, I decided that if conventional presentations were not effective in breaking the dam, maybe a non-conventional approach would. I had an idea: to convey my method through a novel about manufacturing. If people read about lawyers and doctors, why not plant managers? I started to work on The Goal.

Nobody liked it. Not even Jeff Cox, the writer that I hired. He hated it to the extent that he refused to share in the royalties and demanded to be paid cash, in full [...]

The most opposition came from my own people; most refused to read the drafts. I didn't blame them. I was the chief salesman, the prime presenter, the developer. I was the bottleneck, and here I was, wasting my time writing a novel. No, they didn't like it one bit.

I liked it. After thirteen long months of labor, it was finally complete. I was pleased with the results, and thought it was good. The publishers didn't think so. Not the two dozen or so I approached. The most polite rejection I got was from McGraw-Hill: "Dr. Goldratt, if you'd like to write a book about scheduling the shop floor, we'd be delighted to be your publisher. If you want to write a love story, maybe we'll look at it. But a love story about manufacturing?? Forget it! It will never work. We don't even know which shelf to put it on!"

Larry Gadd, the owner of North River Press, was the only spot of light, but even he didn't really encourage me either. He claimed that we'd be lucky to sell the first printing (3000 copies), but since he personally liked the book so much, he would print it nevertheless. And he did. We gave one hundred bound galleys as gifts, and the snowball started to roll.

It's a compliment for an author when people praise his book. It's an even bigger compliment when they recommend it to others. But the ultimate compliment is people buying the book, in quantities, to give as gifts. And that's exactly what happened. "We will not sell even 3000 copies . . ." What a joke!

Our prospect list exploded. It was quite amusing to watch the change in my own people's attitude toward the book. The enthusiastic response of their prospects embarrassed them to the extent that, finally, they read it. Within two months they all had amnesia — each of them claimed that he always was a big supporter of the idea of a novel. I didn't bother to argue.

As cheesy as the novel was, it seemed to capture a lot of people's situations.

Fan letters started to arrive; letters from plant managers attesting to the realism of the book, "The Goal is written specifically about our plant. We can even tell you the real names of the characters." Some even accused me of hiding in their factory.

It wasn't long before the letters started to detail actual results. One plant manager wrote, "Your book is not a novel anymore — now it's a documentary. We followed Alex Rogo's actions to the letter and we replicated his results exactly. Currently, the only difference between your book and my reality is that my wife didn't come back yet." Many letters included an invitation to come and visit, which I sometimes did.

After this book took off, Goldratt got fired from his job, because people realised that they could apply his ideas without needing his software, something he conceded in this essay. There's something really ironic about the fact that Goldratt didn't make his company achieve The Goal, which, might I remind you in case you have forgotten is: to make money, now and in the future.

I can't help but wonder. Has this book changed me? Will I be more of a systems thinker now? I'm not sure. But I know now, that persuasion can take many forms, and sometimes it's okay to be completely hokey, completely unserious, if it means I can be effective and reach more people.

  1. The Bookhive on Church Street is a gem. ↩

entry.title: (#2026-W40) conferences, meetups, marathis and matcha
entry.content:
The week started with my first time attending IndiaFOSS. ¶

There were so many people everywhere. I’d promised myself that I would wake up early and reach the Centre on time, but I was up till 2AM the night before planning out which talks I would attend. I ended up rushing to the Centre, slapping on an intro sticker on my shirt and reaching Hall 1 just in time for the introduction. ¶

As soon as the introduction finished, people started rushing to their next-scheduled talks. There were multiple discussions happening simultaneously, across different rooms and different topics. My own calendar had multiple overlapping events, and soon I was moving to attend my first proper IndiaFOSS talk. ¶

There were so many events. Speakers were talking about hardware, design, security, and God knows what else. People listened intently and laughed at niche references. Some people were wearing LED badges with animated text. There were nerds everywhere, and it was hard to believe that being a nerd was ever considered uncool. ¶

It’s crazy how many rabbit holes people have gone through, and how deeply they have studied the smallest parts in tech and become experts. One of the talks I attended was in the Documentation Devroom, titled “Python Now Speaks Tamil: Getting Official Docs Translated for a Mother Tongue”. This is how I learned that there’s a community around documentation called Write the Docs and, more specifically, a Tamil Python community called PyTamil. What in the world. ¶

There was another talk from the same devroom called “404: Empathy Not Found” which I enjoyed immensely. It talked about understanding where the user is coming from and what they might need from the documentation to fulfil their problem. I was really impressed by the Documentation Devroom overall. ¶

The talk I liked the most though, was “My zero-to-hero journey deploying a fiber-optic and wireless community mesh” by Kiran Jonnalagadda. This was one I wasn’t planning to attend, but I ended up in the right Hall at the right time to witness Kiran narrating his chronicles to get Wi-Fi in the middle of nowhere. It was practically a show-and-tell, because he was carrying literally everything he was talking about on-stage — from a kilometer of fiber optic to an aluminium weatherbox. If you get the time I’d recommend you watch the recording. ¶

The corridors outside the auditoriums were their own world. There were booths everywhere, with 3D-printed demonstrations and people enthusiastically talking about their projects. TV’s showed a variety of different software demos, and I took pictures of as many as I could to look at later. ¶

One of the booths showed those scanning contraptions used by the Internet Archive to scan books, and I soon learned that it was a more affordable version made by an Indian community (called Servants of Knowledge) to archive old Indian literature. ¶

This is one of those things I feel glad technology exists for. Scriptures that were slowly being consumed by time could now be witnessed by many people, for generations to come. It was also relieving to see their work after the monstrosity that Anthropic is doing just to gather data from old rare books. The polarity in behaviour towards books is incomprehensible. ¶

On a different note, another booth was from a group of students from a school, coming to present their project to the crowd. From what I can remember, it was an assistive typing test game that would progressively get harder and introduce more characters. I found it fun and they asked me to leave feedback for them in a notebook. Here’s their GitHub repository if you want to check it out. ¶

I do wonder if the kids used LLM’s to code, though. I would be sad if they did. School is the age for them to stumble and learn. There would be nothing for them to learn if the code is just spit out by a black box. But they were definitely enthusiastic about the project, and had rehearsed their demo very well. ¶

Stepping out from the Centre for chai had me standing in front of a small pop-up bookshop. I scoured around and judged books by their covers. I was impressed by every single one of them; they were all curated to be on-topic for a convention that revolves around public building, shared resources and conscious living. I loved it. ¶

After attending all the talks I had marked out, collecting merch from some of the booths and meeting some people from IndieWebClub in passing (Priyanshu, Tanvi, Nithilan and Harsh, all on their own IndiaFOSS journeys), I dipped from the conference and met up with Marathi Gang for a late lunch. ¶

We caught up on our individual shenanigans and plans, after which I made a visit to my relatives and went out on an evening walk with them. Looking back, I can’t believe how long this specific day was. I just remember my legs hurting from the exertion and going into a very peaceful sleep afterwards. It was an amazingly extroverted day. ¶

On Sunday, I woke up feeling completely exhausted. I can’t remember how many hours I continued to lie on the bed after waking up. All that to say, I couldn’t attend the second day of IndiaFOSS. I instead watched the livestreams of my bookmarked events while I worked on my own projects and chilled. ¶

The weekdays went by in a flash, working and chatting with coworkers during breaks. I remember feeling the workdays were shorter because of the long weekend coming up, and I looked forward to the three-day holiday. Thank you Gandhi Ji. ¶

I also got some writing done this week, and published some long-pending drafts. I wrote a letter to my college juniors and finally published the results of my comparison of chai premixes. I’m proud of them both. ¶

The hope was to finish all my pending drafts in October, but then I realized the “Facets” on my about page and the “Stories” of my individual projects still need to be written. So the new target is to have the website content properly complete by the end of this year. :) ¶

Friday night was a dinner with Marathi Gang, which later converted into a late-night movie watch (Shang-Chi to be specific, which was a great watch). ¶

I also finished watching Loki this week, and man… what a show. I tend to love shows that revolve around/mess with the concept of time. And this show did it in a really coherent way. I realized I’d never really thought of multiverses and different timelines existing at the same time, but I can see just how complicated it would make… everything. I wonder if we’re living in a “Sacred Timeline” of our own, in which case it’s even rarer for us to exist. ¶

Saturday was spent at IndieWebClub and catching up with IndieFriends afterward. Every meetup makes me even more glad I’m a part of this place. So many ambitious people every single time, always doing something exciting (and are excited to talk about it). I always leave with a fresh plate of thoughts and ideas. ¶

Now, not to scare you, but I’m about to include a Sunday in a weeknote that usually only spans till Saturday. I’m sure you’re thinking “No way! That breaks the format!” I know I know, but thankfully it’s my website and I make the format. So yeah, phew. We’re safe for now. ¶

On Sunday, I went to Jatan’s WeBlog Workshop at Atta Galatta. The workshop was more writing-focused with an intentionally small crowd, for more tight-knit interactions. ¶

I was happy to receive an invitation from Jatan when I did. I didn’t end up writing much during the workshop (I’m realizing my writing process is more so a solo one), but it was still great to meet some old friends and new people on the weekend. ¶

Oh and last thing: I finally tried matcha this weekend. I’ve sort of been prejudiced to it because I thought I’d be labeled a performative male if I had it. But I thought I should atleast give it a proper chance. So after WeBlog we went to anāma, which was right next to Atta Galatta. ¶

Aand… I thought it was okay. I wish I had a less lukewarm take, but I don’t. I first told the group that I thought it was bland, to which I was told I can have sugar added to it. So I realized that’s not a problem. But I still didn’t warm up to it. It wasn’t until Divjot mentioned that the caffeine from matcha is slower-setting than coffee, which made me realize that my ADHD-ish ass can have it as an alternative to coffee1. ¶

So that’s my takeaway. I might have it again. Also the color is pretty. I like green a lot. ¶

With this, I’ve now reached 30 completed weeknotes on the site. That’s a lot of notes. I recently mentioned in IndieWebClub that I write these now because every week leaves a footprint; there’s evidence that the week happened and that I did something during the week. I stand by that completely, and I hope to continue this practice (even if some weeknotes end up being late). ¶

This week left quite the footprint too. Thank you for reading through. I’ll leave you with some cool content to consume. Peace and love. ¶

entry.title: Why Women Don’t Keep Their Bags in the Overhead Compartment
entry.content:
Bombay, India.

Lately, I’ve been taking the AC train to CST railway station every day. The whole train is always packed, no matter where you're boarding in the morning. Since all the bogies are passage-way connected, sometimes I board from the men’s coach and sometimes, from the ladies’ coach. The AC trains are smaller in terms of seating capacity. So you can't have a 4th seat (a half seat) the way you would in a regular local.

What this also means is that there's less space overhead to keep your bags.

The men's compartment's overhead, I’ve noticed, has been fully optimised by its passengers to store their bags. A couple of gentlemen on the 9:10 am train even bring extra strong S-hooks to hang extra bags for their fellow passengers. Their bags are organised like books on a library shelf. Neck to neck, vertically, their spines visible neatly.

But the overheads in the ladies’ compartment often sit only half-full in a hellishly packed coach. Most women carry their bags on their front, even laptop bags, since it is more convenient for boarding and alighting. The practicality behind this is one of the oldest and largest unspoken understandings in Bombay commuter culture.

Women, once boarded, seldom let go of their bags. I’ve seen them keep their bags down on the train floor instead of depositing them in the overheads even if they're standing all the way to the very last stop.

This has not gone unnoticed by men in the adjacent coach, who, because of the connected bogies, have seen the shelves half-full. I’ve heard their banter. “Women and their obsession with their bags, I tell you,” one S-hook uncle guffawed with his other bag-free brethren as though this were just one long afternoon tea, and not an intimacy lesson on how armpits smell in an AC box.

I think fundamentally this stark visible contrast speaks to me of the most familiar relationship women have with hypervigilance. We've had things taken away from us so often, we maybe subconsciously just assume we're going to lose our water bottles, our dabbas or a magazine the same way we’ve often lost agency over our minds and bodies, without notice, and to the silent violences of being forced to negotiate with “No”.

For many women like me (I include trans and nonbinary folks in my definition), bags have been the first line of defence against being groped. A friend I was speaking to about this piece told me how they always boarded with their bags to the front to restrict or block access to their breasts. As someone with large breasts, I’ve often used multiple bags to block access to being perceived as someone who has them. Sometimes I carry a jacket in the smouldering heat for the same reason.

I still carry the relief of masks being normalised post-COVID. It was strange to feel safe in public during a pandemic because social distancing restricted access to the physical space around my body and masks protected me from being perceived.

There are, of course, practical reasons for not using the overheads. Some of us do need more things, more sips of water, a wipe. Many put on makeup on the way, because beauty standards mean there are more things to carry here too; many work on the way; many write journals on the way.

And I want to linger on the “more things” for a second. I once heard a gym bro in a video tell his partner not to worry about her tummy fat because her body had more organs to protect. His consideration lingered with me in the warmer places of my heart.

Since government policy and the uncles who love telling me my gender love biological reductionism, where is the consideration that the bodies they are so invested in categorising might also have material needs?

Many menstruators sweat more on their period, so they need quicker access to a wet wipe. Pain is a constant, so a bulky, portable hot water bag? Yes. I have more neck and shoulder strain from breast tenderness, so I often carry a neck pillow for the long ride. These things do not exist in some abstract category of “women’s things”. They are objects required to negotiate a body in the world.

Depositing this world of needs on the overhead cuts off ease of access to it. So we hold our worlds close to our chest.

In this liminal space in the ladies’ compartment—between working for no money at home and working for some money in an office—many women live for themselves. We see entire communities form in these trains. Sony once made a TV show called Ladies Special about the Ladies Special local trains, like the one that runs between Kalyan and CST, where women formed intense friendships that are deeply untangled from their familial lives.

It is telling that even in the thrall of this community, women find it difficult to let go of what is more familiar than any found family: our respective hypervigilances.

Sometimes I am hopeful that hypervigilance has a moment to retire when I see women hand their bags over to other women to just hold, not even place them in the overhead compartment, but just hold them like they are trusting each other with themselves. In that space I glimpse the rare trust that what belongs to them might just stay theirs in the hands of another.

In light of women taking to the streets in India yet again to ask for the right to take up space in the country, with the revolution sitting in our hands amid so many questions of "Why didn't she report this?" I look at the bags placed in the overheads of the train in the men's compartment and at the bags held on for life in the women's compartment as a visual example of the corrosive, intimate, and ultimately most familiar relationship women share with hypervigilance.

Sometimes, even in the hands of their trusted train-friends, some women’s eyes still return to their bags ever so often, through sheer reflex from decades of wearing armour.

The hypervigilance never alights from the train.
